comment_text.value:
Godel's incompleteness and the Halting problem preclude an unbreakable system. Any certificate that code is bug free, secure, has no back doors, halts, etc. is doomed to fail, in general, for systems that are complex enough.

The situation is, theoretically, much worse, where one can even embed backdoors into the compilers themselves and then have the backdoor propagate undetected in perpetuity . This has been known for a long time and Ken Thompson had a famous article "Reflections on Trusting Trust" (1984) [0] that talks about this issue.

In practice, this tends to be very difficult. Extra functionality introduces bloat and complexity. Obfuscation needs to be de-obfuscated by some method, usually known methods. Open source, many eyes, re-implementation and observation and mitigation tend to catch these issues.

Vulnerabilities (in my opinion) tend to get introduced from unintended behavior (bugs) and, very rarely, through directed premeditated malicious action (supply chain attacks, say). Unintended behavior can be exploited by attackers but wasn't introduced with the intent of obfuscation, whereas malice action tends to try and hide themselves.

There's no silver bullet. The best we can do is try to create systems that have certificates of security where we can (for, say restricted computation models) and create empirical tests and responses for the rest. For example, SQL is Turning machine equivalent, so the way around running into the halting problem is to have a timeout that will fail when triggered and leave it up to the user to create a query that runs under time constraints.

You come from biology, so you should know better than most that our body is under constant assault from foreign invaders. Some viruses come in and rewrite code that can then sneak past the immune response, replicate themselves, etc. Our body has evolved a bunch of empirical responses to such malicious action. "Cell not communicating properly?" kill it. "We're under attack?" chop up the invader to get identifying signatures for a counterattack. I'm sure you know better than me all the intricate and complicated ways our immune system handles attacks. It's not perfect, but it does pretty well, considering.

I think there is a contingent of computer scientists and software developers that we should only be using restricted computation models for critical software, so that we can reason about what the software does. This effectively sidesteps Godel's incompleteness/Halting problem because it's not general computing. My feeling is those are, as well, doomed to failure as Turing machine completeness is the norm and very hard to avoid and any system that's so crippled as to not be Turing machine equivalent has limited use.

[0] https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~rdriley/487/papers/Thompson_1984_Ref...

comment_text.value: This is not super surprising to me and mirrors my own experience with Astra and other models. I believe there is a more prosaic explanation: it is not obstructing safety research because it will restrict Astra's power in the future, its doing it because this is a type of research with overall safety implications that it has been trained to detect and avoid. So in other words, I believe this will also happen in the context of bio research. This aversion to certain tasks deemed dangerous is introduced in post-training, so that part of the explanation is parsimonious as well. While Claude will explicitly downgrade you for [bio], [cyber], or [frontier_llm] Astra may be more prone to silent obfuscation on similarly "dangerous" tasks.

story_title.value: GPT-6 Astra covertly underperforms on safety research

comment_text.value: Shannon's entropy theory disagrees. No matter how good the best AI is, its ability to hide a backdoor is limited by the information density within the programming language, and the complexity of possible backdoors will plateau, allowing much lesser AIs to discover them. Consider that binary software is just a more dense form of code, too. A much less dense form, Javascript, makes finding backdoors easy because they all have to use obfuscation via base64 or something to avoid static analysis, which itself immediately draws suspicion.

comment_text.value:
Agree, it makes sense, a lot of people are catching on to LLMs for reverse engineering finally, but its been possible. LLMs can and will eventually flawlessly dissect models. I experiment with Claude, I ask it tasks I know are possible, but have no idea the solution, it can reverse engineer obfuscated projects faster than most talented people I know in that field (talking about games now not AI). I heard a developer say their latest release would take at least a month to figure out the obfuscation and encryption, Opus 5 did it in like... 15 minutes of talking to me (I did throw it the right questions / suggestions). I do that all in the name of seeing just exactly what is possible.

Claude has been able to do reverse engineering for nearly a year if not longer, as well as full source code rewrites, if you know how to do a proper rewrite, luckily for me, most of my career has been rewrites.

story_title.value: The 'Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen' post is misleading
